clinicalPearls: An ophthalmic emergency caused by giant cell (temporal) arteritis, occurring almost exclusively in patients over 50 and typically over 70.
Visual loss is usually severe, frequently counting fingers or worse, and may be preceded by transient obscurations (amaurosis fugax).
The swollen disc is characteristically chalky-white and pallid, in contrast to the hyperaemic oedema of the non-arteritic form.
Systemic features include jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, polymyalgia rheumatica, malaise, weight loss and fever.
Inflammatory markers are markedly raised, with high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein and often a reactive thrombocytosis.
High-dose systemic corticosteroids must be started immediately on clinical suspicion to protect the fellow eye, without waiting for biopsy.
Temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis but skip lesions occur, so a negative biopsy does not exclude the disease and treatment should not be delayed.
A concurrent cilioretinal artery occlusion may accompany the optic nerve head infarction and is highly suggestive of an arteritic mechanism.
reference.pathophysiology: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries with a predilection for branches of the external and internal carotid arteries, including the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the anterior optic nerve head. Inflammatory infiltration disrupts the internal elastic lamina, with giant cells and intimal hyperplasia narrowing and occluding the lumen. The resulting thrombotic occlusion produces infarction of the optic nerve head, and the widespread vascular involvement explains the high risk of rapid, bilateral, and often devastating visual loss.
additionalDifferentials: Other systemic vasculitides affecting the eye
Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, ideally before starting steroids but never delaying treatment
Full blood count for thrombocytosis and anaemia of chronic disease
Temporal artery biopsy of an adequate length segment
Colour Doppler ultrasonography of the temporal arteries seeking the halo sign
Fluorescein angiography showing delayed or patchy choroidal filling
Large-vessel imaging such as positron emission tomography or magnetic resonance angiography where extracranial involvement is suspected
redFlags: Any systemic symptoms of giant cell arteritis in an older patient with visual loss
Transient visual obscurations preceding fixed loss, signalling imminent infarction
Symptoms in the fellow eye indicating impending bilateral blindness
New diplopia or ocular motor palsy accompanying visual loss
reference.prognosis: Visual loss in the affected eye is usually severe and permanent, with meaningful recovery rare. Prompt high-dose corticosteroid therapy is highly effective at preventing catastrophic fellow-eye involvement, which is the principal goal of treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate excludes the disease, when C-reactive protein and platelets may still be raised
Delaying corticosteroids to await biopsy and risking bilateral blindness
Treating with an inadequate corticosteroid dose or tapering too quickly
Missing occult giant cell arteritis presenting with visual loss and few or no systemic symptoms
references: British Society for Rheumatology guideline on the management of giant cell arteritis
management: Immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids on clinical suspicion without waiting for biopsy, using intravenous methylprednisolone for visual loss followed by oral prednisolone, principally to protect the fellow eye
Confirm the diagnosis with temporal artery biopsy or temporal artery ultrasound, ideally soon after starting steroids so treatment is not delayed
Slow corticosteroid taper guided by symptoms and inflammatory markers over many months
Steroid-sparing therapy with the interleukin-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab to reduce relapse and cumulative steroid exposure
Bone protection with a bisphosphonate and calcium and vitamin D, gastroprotection, and glycaemic monitoring during prolonged steroids, with low-dose aspirin in selected patients
Monitor for relapse and large-vessel complications such as aortitis
Low-vision rehabilitation for established visual loss, with urgent rheumatology and ophthalmology referral
